'''Margaret "Maggie" Lowe Benston''' (1937&ndash;1991) was a professor of [[chemistry]], [[computing science]], and [[women's studies]] at [[Simon Fraser University]] in [[Vancouver]], [[British Columbia]], Canada.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.sfu.ca/archives2/F-69/F-69.html |title=Maggie Benston collection |last1=Cox |first1=Sue |year=1983 |website=Simon Fraser University Archives |publisher=Simon Fraser University |location=Vancouver, British Columbia, Canada |access-date=July 1, 2014 |archive-date=September 24, 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150924100959/http://www.sfu.ca/archives2/F-69/F-69.html |url-status=live }}</ref> She was a respected feminist and labour activist, as well as a founding member of the [[Vancouver Women's Caucus]], in 1988, the Euphoniously Feminist and Non-Performing Quintet in 1970, Simon Fraser University's Women's Studies Program in 1975, and Mayworks in 1988.<ref name="Letters to Maggie">{{cite book|last1=Portrebenko|first1=Helen|title=Letters to Maggie|date=1998|publisher=Lazara Press|location=Vancouver|isbn=978-0920999349}}</ref> For thirty years, Benston worked locally, nationally, and internationally writing articles, giving speeches, and lobbying politicians on behalf of the women's and labour movement.<ref name=MLBLectureSeries>{{cite web|website=Simon Fraser University - Department of Gender, Sexuality, and Women’s Studies|title=Margaret Lowe Benston (MLB) Lecture Series in Social Justice (1995-2008) - Summary|year=2008|url=http://summit.sfu.ca/item/10627|access-date=2014-10-15|archive-date=2015-10-28|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151028104605/http://summit.sfu.ca/item/10627|url-status=live}}</ref> Benston died of cancer on 7 March 1991.<ref name=Obituary>{{cite journal | last = Balka | first = Ellen | title = Margaret Lowe Benston: 1937-1991 | journal = [[Labour/Le Travail|Labour]] | volume = 28 | pages = 11&ndash;13 | publisher = [[Canadian Historical Association#Activities|Canadian Committee on Labour History]] (CCLH) | jstor = 25143505 | date = Fall 1991 | url = https://journals.lib.unb.ca/index.php/LLT/article/viewFile/4811/5684 }}</ref>

== Academic work ==

Margaret Benston obtained an undergraduate degree in chemistry and philosophy and a PhD in theoretical chemistry from the [[University of Washington]] in 1964.<ref name=Lowe1993>{{cite journal | last = Lowe | first = Marian | title = To understand the world in order to change it | journal = [[Canadian Woman Studies]] | volume = 13 | issue = 2 | pages = 6&ndash;10 | publisher = [[Inanna Publications]] | date = Winter 1993 | url = https://cws.journals.yorku.ca/index.php/cws/article/viewFile/10441/9530 | archive-date = 2018-01-10 | access-date = 2018-01-10 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20180110174442/https://cws.journals.yorku.ca/index.php/cws/article/viewFile/10441/9530 | url-status = live }}</ref><ref name="Political Economy" /> Following this, she worked as a post-doctoral student at the University of Wisconsin.<ref name="Lowe1993" />  Benston joined Simon Fraser University as a charter faculty member in 1966 in the Department of Chemistry. She was one of the founders of Women's Studies program in the mid-1970s, and taught in the program part-time.  Best known for articles such as "Infrared Spectroscopy" in ''The Annual Review of Physical Chemistry'' and "New Force Theorem" in ''The Journal of Chemistry and Physics,'' Benston continued as a practicing scientist throughout her life, but also went on to be more involved in feminism and activism.<ref name="Political Economy" />  Her 1969 essay, ''The Political Economy of Women's Liberation'', was one of the first [[Marxist feminist]] critiques from a Canadian perspective.<ref>{{cite journal | last = Holmstrom | first = Nancy | title = The Socialist Feminist Project | journal = [[Monthly Review]] | volume = 54 | issue = 10 | pages = 38 | doi = 10.14452/mr-054-10-2003-03_4 | date = March 2003 }}</ref> This article helped establish the framework for much of the feminist debates in the 1970s, as it was one of the first to use a Marxist parameter to explain the oppression of women.<ref name="Obituary"/> The article was later reproduced in books such as ''Liberation Now? Women in a Made-Made World'' and ''Feminist Frameworks'', it was also translated into Spanish, French, Italian, Swedish, German, and Japanese.<ref name="Political Economy">{{cite journal | last1 = Luxton | first1 = Meg | last2 = Armstrong | first2 = Pat | title = Margaret Lowe Benston, 1937–1991 | journal = [[Studies in Political Economy|Studies in Political Economy: A Socialist Review]] | volume = 35 | issue = 1 | pages = 7&ndash;11 | doi = 10.1080/19187033.1991.11675449 | date = 1991 }}</ref>

In the 1980s, Benston became interested in [[computer science]]. She switched fields and received a joint appointment in the Women's Studies and Computing Science departments. Thereafter she explored the relationship between computerization, women, and work.<ref name="sfnews">{{cite news |author=<!--Staff writer(s); no by-line.--> |title=Who was Maggie Benston? |url=https://www.sfu.ca/archive-sfunews/sfnews/1996/Sept19/benston.html |newspaper=Simon Fraser News |location=Vancouver, British Columbia, Canada |publisher=Simon Fraser University |date=September 19, 1996 |volume=7 |number=2 |access-date=July 1, 2014 |archive-date=March 4, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304071502/http://www.sfu.ca/archive-sfunews/sfnews/1996/Sept19/benston.html |url-status=dead }}</ref>

Benston was the first to argue that women formed a [[reserve army of labour]], a group that could be manipulated in a certain way because women are responsible for the reproduction of labour power. She argued that women's domestic and [[wage labour]] were essential to the flow of capitalist production and that women could not be fully integrated into wage labour without a full transformation in both of the forms of labour, which ultimately would mean a transformation of capitalism. In turn, this created the view that women form a class because of their domestic labour, this became known internationally as the domestic labour debate.<ref name="Political Economy" />

== Personal life and activism ==

Committed to [[social justice]], Benston was a founding member of the Euphoniously Feminist and Non-Performing Quintet, groups who taught feminist labour and anti-war songs to audiences at picket lines and rallies.<ref>{{cite journal | last = Davitt | first = Pat | title = Songs for Ourselves, Revisited: A Dialogue Between Maggie Benston and the Rest of the Euphoniously Feminist and Non-Performing Quintet | journal = [[Canadian Woman Studies]] | volume = 13 | issue = 2 | pages = 21&ndash;24 | publisher = [[Inanna Publications]] | date = Winter 1993 | url = https://cws.journals.yorku.ca/index.php/cws/article/viewFile/10444/9533 | archive-date = 2015-12-23 | access-date = 2018-01-10 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20151223142102/http://cws.journals.yorku.ca/index.php/cws/article/viewFile/10444/9533 | url-status = live }}</ref> As a [[labour activist]], she helped found Vancouver Mayworks (a cultural festival celebrating workers), the Vancouver Women's Caucus, a New Left political craze that swept Simon Fraser University in the late 1960s,<ref name="Clandestine Operations">{{cite journal|last1=Sethna|first1=Christabelle|last2=Hewitt|first2=Steve|title=Clandestine Operations: The Vancouver Women's Caucus, the Abortion Caravan, and the RCMP|journal=The Canadian Historical Review|date=September 2009|volume=90|issue=3|pages=463–495|doi=10.1353/can.0.0189|s2cid=162341115 }}</ref> and Women's Skills Development of British Columbia.<ref name="Obituary" /> A music fan, she played a leading role in establishing the [[Vancouver Folk Music Festival]].<ref name="sfnews" /> Benston also helped start the Vancouver Mayworks, a festival that celebrated workers' culture.<ref name="Political Economy" /> Mayworks is currently a Festival of Labour and the Arts, with active participants in Parksville, Comox Valley and Campbell River, on Vancouver Island.<ref>{{cite web|title=Mayworks| website=[[Facebook]] |url=https://www.facebook.com/pages/MAYWORKS-VANCOUVER-ISLAND/121141981236180?sk=info&ref=page_internal}}</ref>

With five other women (Mary Vickers, Hilda Ching, Abby Schwarz, Mary Jo Duncan, Diana Herbst), Benston founded The [[Society for Canadian Women in Science and Technology]] (SCWIST) in Vancouver in 1981,<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.sfu.ca/archives2/F-39/F-39.html|title=Society for Canadian Women in Science and Technology fonds|website=Simon Fraser University Archives|publisher=Simon Fraser University|location=Vancouver, British Columbia, Canada|volume=13|number=2|access-date=July 1, 2014|archive-date=July 15, 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130715185421/http://www.sfu.ca/archives2/F-39/F-39.html|url-status=live}}</ref>  which aims to "support and promote the education of girls and women through programs and activities that we develop in partnership with the community."<ref name=SCWIST>{{cite web |title =What is SCWIST|url=http://www.scwist.ca/about-scwist/what-is-scwist/|website=scwist.ca|date=5 January 2023 |publisher=[[Society for Canadian Women in Science and Technology]]}}</ref> Benston died in 1991 at age 52, after a long battle with cancer.<ref name="sfnews" />

== Legacy ==

The Maggie Benston Centre at Simon Fraser University was the second campus building named after a woman at the university (the first being the Madge Hogarth residence).<ref name="sfnews" />

The Margaret Lowe Benston Memorial Graduate Bursary in Gender, Sexuality and Women's Studies is named after her.<ref name="SFU">{{cite web |url=https://www.sfu.ca/dean-gradstudies/awards/privateawards/all-awards/benston.html |title=Margaret Lowe Benston Memorial Graduate Bursary in Gender, Sexuality and Women's Studies |website=Graduate Studies & Postdoctoral Fellows: Private Awards |publisher=Simon Fraser University |location=Vancouver, British Columbia, Canada |access-date=July 1, 2014 |archive-date=September 24, 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150924115145/http://www.sfu.ca/dean-gradstudies/awards/privateawards/all-awards/benston.html |url-status=live }}</ref> The purpose of this award is to provide financial support for students in the MA and PhD programs in the Department of Gender, Sexuality, and Women's Studies at Simon Fraser University.<ref name="SFU" />

Begun in 1994, the "Margaret Lowe Benston (MLB) Lecture Series in Social Justice is financed by an endowment established in her memory.<ref name="SFU" />  There is an annual event hosted by the Department of Gender, Sexuality, and Women's Studies at Simon Fraser University.  Events are often lectures but have also included dance performances and film presentations (ex. My Name Was January).  Some past speakers/presenters include [[Alex Sangha]], Elina Gress, Lenee Son, Velvet Steele, and Natasha Adsit (2019), [[Susan Stryker]] (2014), [[Maude Barlow]], Sitara Thobani (2008), Arno Kamolika, [[Doudou Diène]], [[Lisa Helps]], Becki Ross & [[Jamie Lee Hamilton]], Joan Sangster, [[Chris E. Vargas]],  [[Marilyn Waring]] and [[Leslie Feinberg]].<ref name=SFU /> The events continue to be highly successful, having a general attendance of between 200 and 320 people.<ref name="SFU" />
